open-question.question: On a host without a blocking wait, where the orchestrator batches per wake-up, does the dispatch prompt still name a run scratch directory for the agent to write into, so the agent's contract and the prompt are the same on every host, or does the agent choose its own scratch path there and the prompt keep its two values?
open-question.alternative: The orchestrator creates one run scratch directory on every host, including a host without a blocking wait where it batches per wake-up, and passes that directory as a third value in the dispatch prompt beside the Short Title and `<MILESTONE_DIR>`. The dispatch prompt template in `core/skills/provide-alternatives-to-all-open-questions/SKILL.md` and the agent file `core/agents/provide-alternatives-to-open-question.md` stay host-neutral and unconditional: the agent writes its one file into the named directory and returns that file's path. No slot is added and no existing slot carries the directory line, so the waiting sentence stays the only part that differs by host. The agent's contract, the prompt, the agent file, and the `CLAUDE.md` dispatch-prompt invariant read the same in every host tree. The per-wake-up form then differs from the single-wait form only in when the orchestrator embeds, which matches the goal's single host slot. Every return lands in one known place per run, so a batch can be assembled the same way on every host. On a per-wake-up host the orchestrator creates and names a directory that it does not need for waiting, which adds one more value it must create and hold for each dispatch. The orchestrator and the agent must both be able to write to the same directory. On Codex, where temp-directory writability under the sandbox is unrecorded, that is not yet established, and it depends on the sibling question about the scratch directory's location. If the sibling Codex and Antigravity wait-form questions give every host the single-wait form, no per-wake-up host is left and this question is moot.

On a host without a blocking wait the dispatch prompt keeps its two values, Short Title and `<MILESTONE_DIR>`. The directory line appears only in the single-wait hosts' prompt, carried by a per-host value such as the existing `ALTERNATIVES_PROMPT_INSTRUCTIONS` prefix slot or the waiting slot's own wording, so no new slot is declared. The one host-neutral agent file states both cases. If the prompt names a scratch directory, the agent writes its file there. Otherwise it creates its own scratch file outside the repository, for example a fresh temporary file, and returns that path. The per-wake-up host's prompt stays exactly two values, so the orchestrator there creates and holds nothing extra. On a sandboxed host the agent picks a location it can actually write to itself, which avoids a shared directory whose writability is unrecorded. The agent's contract is no longer the same on every host. It carries a branch keyed on whether a value is present, and `CLAUDE.md`, `docs/design-claims.md` claim 13, and the skill reference must describe two prompt shapes. On a per-wake-up host the scratch files of one run are scattered, so the orchestrator learns each path only from the returns. That fits only if the sibling question about scratch file naming and return settles on the agent reporting its path. Placing the directory line in an existing per-host slot also stretches what that slot means, and this interacts with the sibling question about where the waiting wording is placed.

alternative.id: Two values, per-host agent contract slot

open-question.alternative: On a host without a blocking wait the dispatch prompt keeps its two values, as in the conditional option. The difference is in the agent file: the sentence saying where the agent writes becomes a new host slot in `core/agents/provide-alternatives-to-open-question.md`, declared by all three host definitions. Each rendered tree's agent file states only its own case: write into the directory the prompt names on a single-wait host, or choose your own scratch file outside the repository on a per-wake-up host. The prompt's directory line rides a matching per-host value. Each host tree's agent reads one unconditional contract with no branch, and the per-wake-up host still creates and passes nothing beyond today's two values. The build's `slot-declaration` check keeps the per-host wording consistent with the three host definitions. It adds a second host slot, which contradicts the goal's statement that the waiting sentence is the one host slot, so choosing it would mean revising the goal. It also splits the agent file, today free of any wording slot, across hosts. If Antigravity is not given the Claude Code value, that split breaks the byte-identity between the Claude Code and Antigravity trees. Like the conditional option, it depends on the sibling question about scratch file naming and return settling on the agent reporting its path, and it is moot if no host ends up with the per-wake-up form.

open-question.question: When the orchestrator creates the run's scratch directory, where outside the repository does it create it: a fresh temporary directory under the system temp location, the host's session scratchpad, or another place, given that temp-directory writability under the Codex sandbox is unrecorded?
open-question.alternative: The orchestrator creates the run's scratch directory with `mktemp -d`, a fresh uniquely named directory under the system temp location (honouring `$TMPDIR`). Every host tree uses the same wording, so the location adds no host slot. The directory belongs to one run only and no other run reuses it. It follows the precedent already in the workflow: `capture-milestone-principle-updates` makes its snapshot with `mktemp`. It is host-neutral and adds no slot beyond the goal's one waiting slot. Because each run gets an empty directory of its own, two runs never collide and no earlier run's files are in it, so the batch can pick up every file there without first removing stale returns. The repository does not record whether a temp directory outside the workspace is writable under Codex's workspace-write sandbox. If it is not, every Codex agent fails to write its file and the pass falls back to repair and skip on every question. On Claude Code run without permission bypass, writing outside the project may also raise a prompt, and a headless run has no one to answer it. The path is random, so the dispatch prompt has to carry it, which depends on how the sibling question about naming the scratch directory in the prompt is settled.

The orchestrator creates a fresh per-run subdirectory inside the session scratchpad directory when the host provides one. On Claude Code that is the `/private/tmp/claude-<uid>/<project>/<session>/scratchpad` path named in the system prompt. When the host provides no scratchpad, it falls back to a fresh `mktemp -d` under the system temp location. The `core/` wording names the capability ("the session scratchpad the host provides") and not the host, so the Claude Code and Antigravity trees stay byte-identical and no slot is added. On Claude Code it writes into the one location outside the repository that the host sets aside for temporary files in this session. That is the location most likely to be writable without a permission prompt or sandbox refusal, for the orchestrator and for the subagents it dispatches. The scratchpad is session-scoped and not run-scoped, so the per-run subdirectory is still needed to keep two runs in one session apart. The conditional wording ships unchanged to Antigravity and Codex, where nothing in the repository says a scratchpad exists, so those hosts run the fallback, and the fallback has the same unrecorded Codex writability as plain temp. Behaviour also differs by host under wording that reads the same everywhere, which makes the pass harder to reason about and to test.

The orchestrator uses a deterministic directory under the system temp location, derived from the project and milestone, for example `${TMPDIR:-/tmp}/cairn-alternatives-<milestone directory name>`. It creates the directory if absent and clears any files left in it at the start of each run. Every host uses the same wording and no slot is added. The path is known before any dispatch and stays the same across runs. If a run is interrupted, files that landed but were never embedded can still be found and inspected at a predictable place. Because the path is fixed, a prompt or agent rule could name it without the orchestrator generating anything. Two runs against milestones with the same directory name collide: concurrent runs in two worktrees or two clones of one project, or two projects with matching slugs. The start-of-run clearing is an extra destructive step, and if it is skipped, stale returns go into the batch. Codex sandbox writability is just as unrecorded as for any temp location.

The orchestrator creates a fresh per-run subdirectory under a persistent per-user location outside both the repository and the system temp, for example `~/.cache/cairn/<run>`. Every host uses the same wording and no slot is added. The files survive temp cleaning and reboots, so refused or unembedded returns can be inspected long after the run. This is the strongest position if inspecting failed returns matters more than leaving nothing behind. A workspace-write sandbox is even less likely to allow writes under the home directory than under temp, so Codex compatibility becomes more doubtful. No host cleans the location automatically, so directories pile up unless the orchestrator deletes them, which depends on how the sibling scratch-file-cleanup question is settled. It also adds a new path convention that nothing else in the workflow uses.

open-question.question: Is each agent's scratch file name derived from its Short Title by a fixed rule, so the orchestrator knows every path before any agent returns and the agent's final message can be a bare success token, or does the agent choose its own file name and report the path as its final message, so the orchestrator learns the paths only from the returns?
open-question.alternative: Each agent writes its checked elements to a file in the run's scratch directory whose name is the question's Short Title exactly as given, plus a fixed extension (for example `<scratch dir>/<Short Title>.xml`). The agent file states this rule. The orchestrator therefore knows every path at dispatch time without the agent reporting it. On success the agent's final message is a fixed bare token such as `DONE`, and on failure it stays `FAILED: <reason>`. The goal sentence saying the agent ends with the file's path is revised to match. Neither side has to compute anything. The orchestrator and the agent each copy the same Short Title, so they cannot disagree about a path. The final message drops to a few tokens, which is the smallest context cost per return. Because every path is known before anything lands, a blocking wait can test for each expected file directly. The open-question tool puts no limit on which characters a Short Title may contain, so a title with a `/` or another character that is unsafe in a path breaks the rule. Titles with spaces also need careful quoting in every shell command that names them. The milestone's goal currently says the agent ends with the path, so this option needs a goal revision. Whether the precomputed paths help the wait depends on how the sibling question about the wait's completion and failure test settles.

Each agent names its scratch file with a normalized slug of its Short Title: ASCII-folded, lowercased, and every run of characters other than letters and digits turned into a hyphen, in the style of the milestone-definition tool's slug. The fixed extension is added, and the rule is stated in the agent file. Separately, the orchestrator applies the same rule to know every path at dispatch time. On success the agent's final message is a fixed bare token, and on failure it stays `FAILED: <reason>`. The goal sentence about returning the path is revised to match. File names are always safe in a path and need no quoting. They stay readable when someone inspects a refused return. The final message is still a bare token, and every path is still known before any agent returns. Short Titles are unique only as written, so two titles that differ only in punctuation or case would get the same slug and overwrite each other's file. No tool exposes the slug rule for arbitrary strings, so the orchestrator and each agent work it out separately by reasoning. A mismatch between them leaves a file the orchestrator never finds. It also needs a goal revision, and the value of knowing paths upfront depends on the sibling question about the wait's completion test.

Each agent names its scratch file with a digest of its Short Title computed by one fixed shell command that the agent file states (for example `printf '%s' "<Short Title>" | shasum`), plus the fixed extension. The orchestrator runs the same command for each dispatched title to know every path before any agent returns. On success the final message is a fixed bare token, and on failure it stays `FAILED: <reason>`. The goal sentence about returning the path is revised to match. Both sides derive the name by running the same command rather than by reasoning, so they always agree. The names are path-safe whatever the Short Title contains, and two distinct titles do not realistically collide. It keeps the bare-token return and upfront knowledge of every path. The names are opaque, so inspecting a refused or leftover file means mapping digests back to titles. Each agent and the batch call need an extra hashing step, which adds shell lines that the "write commands literally" rule then governs. It needs a goal revision, and how much upfront paths are worth depends on the sibling question about the wait's completion test.

The scratch file name follows a fixed rule from the Short Title, stated in the agent file. It is the title verbatim plus a fixed extension; a slug or digest rule trades the same way here, because the returned path is the authoritative one. The agent still ends its session with that file's path as its final message, as the goal is written now, or with `FAILED: <reason>`. The orchestrator can predict every path before returns land, and it pipes the path each return reports. It keeps the goal's return contract unchanged, so no goal revision is needed. A wait can still check expected paths before any return arrives. Because each return names its own file, a rule the agent slipped on is caught rather than leaving a file silently missing. The final message carries a path the orchestrator could already compute, so each return costs more context than a bare token. The project then has two sources for the same fact, and the orchestrator must decide which one wins when they disagree. Whether the predicted paths are used at all depends on the sibling question about the wait's completion test.

No naming rule exists. Each agent creates its own file inside the scratch location under a name of its choosing, for example a unique temporary name. It ends its session with that file's path as its final message, or with `FAILED: <reason>`. The orchestrator learns each path only from the returns and matches each one to its Short Title through the dispatch it came from. The goal sentence stays as written. This is the goal as currently written. The agent file needs no naming rule, and neither side derives anything. Names are path-safe and collision-free by construction, whatever the Short Titles contain. The orchestrator cannot know any path before a return lands. A blocking wait therefore cannot check for specific files and has to rely on a file count or the host's own completion signal, which the sibling question on the wait's completion and failure test decides. The orchestrator must also keep the link from each return to its Short Title, because the file name carries no title. If that link is missing on a host, the batch call cannot name the block to embed into.

The orchestrator builds each agent's full scratch file path itself (for example the scratch directory plus a name derived from the Short Title or from the agent's dispatch position) and passes it in the dispatch prompt as a further value. The agent writes to exactly that path, so the agent file states no naming rule. On success the agent ends with a fixed bare token, and on failure with `FAILED: <reason>`. The goal sentence about returning the path is revised to match. The naming rule lives in one place only, the orchestrator, so the two sides can never derive different paths. Any naming scheme works, dispatch-position numbers included. Every path is known upfront, and the final message stays a bare token. It adds a third value to the dispatch prompt that the agent could otherwise compute itself. That reverses the CLAUDE.md invariant that a prompt carries only what the agent cannot fetch, and it changes the prompt contract on every host. It is viable only alongside however the sibling question on naming the scratch directory in the prompt settles. It also needs a goal revision.

open-question.question: In the single-wait form, what does the blocking wait test to decide that every dispatched agent has finished, and how does an agent that ends with FAILED and writes no elements become visible to that test: a failure marker it writes beside the other files, a bounded wait that gives up, or the host's own completion signal?

Which Claude Code primitive is the blocking wait: a foreground shell loop inside one tool call under its ten-minute cap, a background shell loop or Monitor that returns at once and notifies later, or something else, given that a foreground sleep ran when tested although the host states foreground sleep is blocked?

What does the orchestrator do when the blocking wait ends before every dispatched agent has finished: embed and commit what has landed and wait again, fall back to per-wake-up batching for the rest, or treat the unfinished agents as skipped?
open-question.alternative: When the blocking wait ends with agents still unfinished, the orchestrator pipes every file that has landed so far into one `embed --alternatives` batch and commits each question that embedded, in one shell call. It then issues the same blocking wait again for the agents still outstanding, and repeats until every dispatched agent has landed a file or ended in a failure. No limit is set on how many times it waits again, nothing is skipped because of an expiry, and the run keeps the single-wait form throughout. Finished work is committed at every expiry, so a slow agent never holds the rest hostage and an interrupted run loses only uncommitted returns. Each expiry adds just one batch-plus-wait turn pair, and the run stays in one waiting form on one host. A hung agent keeps the run waiting forever unless the wait's completion test turns it into a failure some other way (the sibling "Wait completion and failure test" owns that). A run with several expiries also makes several batch calls, so the goal's "wakes once per run" holds only when nothing expires.

alternative.id: Embed landed, wait bounded times, then skip

open-question.alternative: At each expiry the orchestrator embeds and commits every landed file in one shell call, then waits again for the outstanding agents. It does this up to a fixed number of further waits (or a fixed total waiting time). After the last allowed wait it embeds whatever has landed and treats every agent still unfinished as skipped. Those questions are listed in the step-4 still-skipped advisory, and a later run of the pass picks them up because their blocks still carry no alternatives. The run's length is bounded, so a hung or runaway agent cannot stall the pass, and slow but healthy agents still get several chances to land. Committed progress accumulates at every expiry. It adds a tunable bound (a count or a duration) to the prose, and that bound has to be justified per host. An agent skipped at the bound may still finish later and write a file that nothing embeds, wasting its tokens and leaving an orphan in the scratch directory. It also stretches the skip from "refused after repair" to "too slow", which changes what the advisory means.

alternative.id: Hold landed, wait again until all land

open-question.alternative: At an expiry the orchestrator embeds nothing. It just issues the blocking wait again for the outstanding agents, with no limit, so every landed file stays in the scratch directory until the whole set has landed or failed. Then it embeds and commits the whole set in the one batch shell call the goal describes. An expiry is invisible to the batching: the run still makes exactly one embed-and-commit call. It keeps the goal's single-wake, single-batch shape exactly, whatever the host's wait cap. The orchestrator adds no branch, only a repeated wait, which is the smallest change to the waiting sentence. Nothing is committed until the slowest agent finishes, so an orchestrator that dies or is interrupted mid-wait commits none of the landed work, and a re-run re-dispatches every bare block. A hung agent stalls the whole run unless the wait's completion test (owned by the sibling "Wait completion and failure test") ends it some other way.

alternative.id: Hold landed, wait bounded times, then batch and skip

open-question.alternative: At an expiry the orchestrator embeds nothing and waits again, up to a fixed number of further waits (or a fixed total waiting time). When every agent has landed or failed, or the bound is reached, it embeds and commits every landed file in one batch shell call. Any agent still unfinished at the bound is treated as skipped and reported in the step-4 still-skipped advisory, to be picked up by a later run of the pass. It keeps exactly one embed-and-commit call per run and still bounds how long the run can last, so neither a long wait cap nor a hung agent changes the batch shape or stalls the pass forever. Landed work stays uncommitted for the whole bounded window, so an interruption loses all of it. It adds a tunable bound, and skipping slow agents leaves orphan files and wasted agent tokens just as the progressive bounded form does.

alternative.id: Embed landed, switch to per-wake-up batching

open-question.alternative: At the first expiry the orchestrator embeds and commits every landed file in one shell call. It then drops the blocking wait for the rest of the run and handles the outstanding agents the way a host without a blocking wait does: it batches every landed return each time it wakes on the host's own completion signal, until every agent has landed or failed. The single-wait form covers the first window, and the per-wake-up form covers whatever is left after it. It reuses the per-wake-up path the goal already writes for hosts without a blocking wait, so expiry needs no new waiting logic. The orchestrator stops blocking on a tool call it cannot extend, and slow agents are still embedded as they finish. Both waiting forms have to be live and correct on the same host within one run, so the waiting sentence must describe the hand-off between them. It works only where the host also delivers per-agent completion wake-ups, which depends on which primitive the sibling "Claude Code wait primitive" picks and on what the siblings "Codex wait form" and "Antigravity wait form" settle. After the switch the run returns to several wake-ups, some of them turns that do nothing.

When the wait ends early, the orchestrator embeds and commits every landed file in one shell call and treats every agent still unfinished as skipped. It neither waits again nor switches form. The skipped questions are listed in the step-4 still-skipped advisory, and their blocks stay bare, so the next run of the pass dispatches them afresh. It is the simplest rule and keeps the run to exactly one wait and one batch, with a hard ceiling on run time set by the host's wait cap. Recovery is already built in, because the pass's idempotent gather re-selects every bare block on its next run. Any agent slower than one wait cap loses its work every time, so on a host with a short cap (a ten-minute foreground call) a large or slow question can be skipped run after run. Agents still running write files that no one embeds, wasting their tokens, unless the orchestrator also stops them. It also turns "slow" into a skip reason that the existing one-repair-then-skip contract never had.

open-question.question: Does the Codex tree get the single-wait form, waiting on each cap-sized round of agents through Codex's own agent tools, or the per-wake-up value, given its subagent thread cap and that the repository records no Codex waiting tool?

Does the Antigravity tree carry the same waiting sentence as Claude Code, keeping the two trees byte-identical on the assumption that it offers the same wait, or the per-wake-up value, given that the repository records nothing about how Antigravity delivers agent returns?

When a batch call refuses some returns, does the orchestrator send every repair at once and wait for the repaired returns as one further batch, or repair and re-embed each refused return on its own as it comes back?

alternative.id: Repaired returns rejoin the batch stream

open-question.alternative: The moment a batch call refuses some returns, the orchestrator sends every one of that call's repairs together in the same turn: a continuation message to each still-held agent session where the host can do that, or one fresh re-dispatch per question where it cannot. Each repaired return lands in the scratch directory the same way a first return does. From there it gets no special handling and is embedded by the same batching rule as any landed return. On a host with a blocking wait, that means one more wait-and-batch over the repair set, because nothing else is still in flight. On a host without a blocking wait, it means whichever wake-up the repaired return lands in, mixed with first returns that land at the same time. The orchestrator tracks per question only whether that question has had its repair. A repaired return that is refused again goes straight to the per-question skip. Repairs still start immediately after the refusal, as the current skill requires, and are never held back as a second phase. One rule covers every landed return, so the skill gains no second pipeline and no repair-only wording. Each repair also costs no wake-up beyond the ones the ordinary batching already spends. On a single-wait host this rule reduces to exactly one further wait and one further batch call. One batch call can mix first returns, which get repaired when refused, with repaired returns, which get skipped when refused. So the orchestrator has to keep per-question repair state across wake-ups and apply the right outcome to each refusal inside a single call. Whether this works cleanly depends on how the batch-input-selection question decides which files one call pipes, and on whether the scratch-file-naming question gives a repaired return its own path or reuses the first one.

Refused returns are not repaired as they are refused. The orchestrator first embeds and commits every first return. On a single-wait host that is one batch. On a host without a blocking wait it is every wake-up batch until no first return is still in flight. Only then does it send all the held repairs together, through continuation where the host allows it and re-dispatch where it does not. It waits for the whole repaired set, embeds it in one further batch call, and skips every repaired return that is refused again. The run therefore always has exactly two phases: first returns, then one repair round. This reverses the current skill's rule that a repair is never held back and run as a second phase after the last first return has landed. Every batch call holds only one kind of input, so a refusal's outcome is fixed for the whole call: repair in the first phase, skip in the repair round. That keeps the orchestrator's accounting and the skill's prose simplest. On a single-wait host the run costs at most two waits and two batch calls in total. On a host without a blocking wait, the repairs start only after the slowest first return lands, which makes the run longer. Agent session handles also have to be held for the whole first phase before they are used, which raises the chance that a handle is gone and the costlier re-dispatch branch is needed. It also overturns an immediacy rule that CLAUDE.md and the skill currently state, so both need rewording beyond the batch change itself.

Batching applies only to first returns. When a batch call refuses a return, its repair is sent at once. When that repaired return lands in its scratch file, it is embedded with its own `embed --alternatives` call and committed on its own, as in today's per-return pipeline. A repaired return that is refused again is skipped. Several repairs sent from the same batch still run concurrently, but each repaired return is judged and embedded alone as it comes back, never grouped with other returns. Refusals are rare now that the tool does the slicing, so keeping the existing per-return logic for that rare path costs little. Each question's repair-then-skip sequence stays a self-contained unit that can never be mixed up with another question's state, and the current repair wording carries over nearly unchanged. The skill ends up describing two pipelines, a batched one for first returns and a per-return one for repairs. Every repaired return also costs its own orchestrator turn, or turns, and on a single-wait host that breaks the goal's promise of waking once per run whenever any return is refused. Waiting for an individual repaired return on such a host also needs a wait form that the wait-primitive and wait-completion questions may not provide.

open-question.question: Which returns does one batch call pipe: only those the wake-up's notifications or the finished wait named, or every file present in the scratch directory, and in the latter case how does the orchestrator avoid re-piping a file it embedded in an earlier batch?
open-question.alternative: Each batch call takes exactly the scratch files that the returns delivered since the last batch named. In the per-wake-up form, these are the paths in the final messages of the notifications in this wake-up. In the single-wait form, they are the set the finished wait reports. A repaired return joins the batch of the wake-up or wait that delivers it. The orchestrator never lists the scratch directory, so it never tracks which files were already embedded. A file can only be piped twice if the same path is delivered twice. Each return reaches exactly one batch with no extra mechanism and no record on disk or in context. A file is piped only after its agent has ended, so a file still being written is never picked up. The orchestrator also stays tied to the agent's own report, including the FAILED returns that write no file. The orchestrator has to copy each delivered path from the notification or wait output into the shell command, which is one more piece of return text held in context per question. A file that is already in place but whose notification is queued waits for a later wake-up. In the single-wait form, what "the finished wait named" means depends on what the wait reports (the wait completion and failure test sibling owns this). Matching a path to its Short Title depends on the scratch file naming sibling.

Each batch call lists the scratch directory and pipes every file in it, regardless of which notifications arrived. In the same shell call, each file it pipes is moved, whether embed accepted or refused it, to a processed subdirectory or a fixed renamed form. The next scan therefore sees only files that arrived after this batch. A repaired return lands as a new file and is picked up by the next scan. Whether embedded files are later deleted is not changed by this option. The record of what was already piped lives on disk, not in the orchestrator's context. The batch command is one fixed scan-pipe-move loop with no per-path copying, and it also embeds files whose notifications have not arrived yet. This option suits both forms equally. A scan can pick up a file its agent is still writing, unless the agent's write is atomic (write then rename) or the file is complete before its agent ends. The orchestrator still needs the notifications to learn which agents failed without writing a file. The move adds a file operation per question whose fit depends on the scratch file cleanup sibling. Linking a file to its Short Title for the embed call and the commit depends on the scratch file naming sibling.

Each batch call lists the scratch directory and, in the same shell call, pipes only the files whose Short Title still has no alternatives in the question document. It checks this with the open-question tool's list of questions without alternatives. No file is moved and the orchestrator keeps no list. The question document is the only record of what is done. A repaired return replaces or joins the refused file, and its block is still bare, so the next scan picks it up. Nothing is tracked except the document every pass already relies on. Interrupting and resuming the run, or re-running the pass, cannot re-pipe an embedded file. It also cannot pipe a file whose question an earlier batch already annotated. Like the plain scan, it embeds files whose notifications have not arrived yet. A refused file leaves its block bare, so every later scan pipes it and gets the same refusal again. The orchestrator would then have to remember which refusals it already repaired, which brings back the context state the gate was meant to avoid. The option also needs a reversible mapping from file name to Short Title, which depends on the scratch file naming sibling. It has the same risk as the other scans of picking up a file that is still being written.

Each batch call lists the scratch directory and pipes every file except those the orchestrator has already piped earlier in this run. The orchestrator keeps that list in its own context and writes it into each batch command as an exclusion. Nothing on disk is moved or renamed. A repaired return arrives under a path not on the list, or the orchestrator takes the refused path off the list when it sends the repair. It embeds files whose notifications are still queued without touching the scratch files. The rule for what goes into a batch is a plain set difference, computed in the same call. The orchestrator holds and re-types a growing per-run list in context, the kind of work this milestone sets out to remove. Handling the list wrongly, by forgetting or mistyping one path, either re-pipes an embedded file or drops a return. It also has the scan's risk of picking up a file that is still being written. How repaired returns are named on disk depends on the scratch file naming and repair rounds siblings.

Each batch call pipes every file in the scratch directory, with no move and no record. A file embedded in an earlier batch is piped again, and the tool refuses it because its target block already has alternatives. The orchestrator treats that particular refusal as "already embedded" and does not judge it as a failed return, so no repair is triggered. It is the simplest command and needs no state anywhere. It leaves the open-question tool unchanged and relies on a refusal the tool already makes. The pipeline's one-repair rule keys on any embed refusal. So the orchestrator's instructions would have to tell this one refusal apart from a real one, which brings tool error text into the runtime instructions that the project keeps free of tool mechanics. Each batch also re-pipes every earlier file, so the work grows with the run. A file whose return was refused and not yet repaired is piped and refused again on every batch.

open-question.question: Are the scratch files and their directory deleted by the orchestrator, after each successful embed or at the end of the run, or left in place for the host's temp handling and for inspecting refused returns?

alternative.id: Delete each file after its embed, keep refused files

open-question.alternative: The orchestrator deletes each scratch file in the same shell call as the batch that embedded it, as soon as `embed --alternatives` accepts it. Files that were refused, or that belong to a question still skipped after its repair, stay where they are. At the end of the run the orchestrator removes the run's scratch directory only if it is empty, with a non-recursive remove that does nothing when files remain. Whatever is left is handed to the host's temp handling. Only the files that matter for diagnosis survive: each one is a return the tool refused or a question the end-of-run advisory already names as skipped. Deleting at embed time also means a later batch on a per-wake-up host never finds an already-embedded file in the directory to pipe again. It adds a delete step to every batch and a conditional directory removal to the run's end, all in the prose of the one shell call the goal keeps small. The empty-only removal also leaves a directory behind on every run that skipped a question. It needs the orchestrator to know each file's path at embed time, which depends on the naming and scratch-directory-in-prompt siblings.

alternative.id: Delete each file after its embed, remove the directory at run end

open-question.alternative: The orchestrator deletes each scratch file in the same shell call as the batch that embedded it. At the end of the run it removes the whole scratch directory recursively, including any refused or skipped returns still inside it. Nothing from the run outlives it. The run leaves nothing behind wherever the directory lives, whatever the host's temp policy. Per-embed deletion still keeps a later batch from re-piping an embedded file. The one return worth inspecting is destroyed: a refused or skipped return whose `Error:` line the advisory reports, which was the only evidence of why it failed. It adds deletion prose in two places. A recursive remove of a path the orchestrator built is a risky command to write into a runner, and it may raise a permission prompt in a headless chain where no one can answer it.

alternative.id: Remove the whole directory at run end only

open-question.alternative: The orchestrator leaves every scratch file in place while the run is going. After the last batch, and after the commits and any repairs, it removes the run's scratch directory recursively in one command, refused and skipped returns included. Nothing is deleted per embed. Cleanup is one command at one point in the run, separate from the per-batch embed-and-commit call. In the single-wait form, where there is only one batch, it costs exactly what per-embed deletion costs. Refused returns are lost just as in the per-embed variant. On a per-wake-up host, embedded files stay in the directory between batches, so it only works if the batch-input-selection sibling avoids re-piping them some other way. A run that stops early on a tool failure skips the final removal and leaves everything behind anyway.

alternative.id: At run end, delete embedded files and keep refused ones

open-question.alternative: The orchestrator leaves every scratch file in place while the run is going. After the last batch it deletes the files whose questions embedded and keeps the refused or skipped returns. It removes the directory only if it is empty, otherwise leaving it to the host's temp handling. Like per-embed deletion, it keeps the failed returns for inspection, and it collects all cleanup into one end-of-run step instead of spreading it across batches. To delete selectively at the end, the orchestrator has to carry the embedded/refused split through the whole run, which is extra state for an orchestrator meant to hold no work context. On a per-wake-up host, embedded files stay in the directory between batches, so it relies on the batch-input-selection sibling to avoid re-piping them. An early stop leaves everything behind.

alternative.id: No deletion, leave it to host temp handling

open-question.alternative: The orchestrator deletes nothing: no scratch file, no directory, at no point in the run. The run's scratch directory and every return in it, embedded or refused, are left to the host's own temp handling. That could be system temp cleanup or the expiry of the session scratchpad. It is the least runner prose and the fewest commands, with no remove command to word safely or to get a permission prompt in a headless chain. Every return, accepted or refused, can be inspected after the run, the same way the transcripts were mined for the token report. Files pile up across runs at a rate that depends entirely on where the directory lives (the scratch-directory-location sibling), and nothing in the repository records Codex's or Antigravity's temp handling. Copies of milestone content sit outside the repository until something else clears them. On a per-wake-up host, embedded files stay in the directory, so it relies on the batch-input-selection sibling, and on a fresh directory per run, to avoid re-piping a file it already embedded.

open-question.question: Does the waiting wording live in the existing ALTERNATIVES_CONCURRENCY slot, whose values already say how returns are handled as they land, or in a new slot of its own, with the concurrency slot left to say only how many dispatches run at once?
open-question.alternative: The waiting wording goes into the existing ALTERNATIVES_CONCURRENCY slot, which keeps its name and its place at the opening of step 3. Each host's value is rewritten as one paragraph covering how many dispatches run at once, whether the run waits once for every return or batches each time it wakes, and, in the Codex value, when each agent is closed and the next question dispatched. No new slot is declared. ALTERNATIVES_DISPATCH, ALTERNATIVES_PROMPT_INSTRUCTIONS, ALTERNATIVES_AGENT, and AGENT_TOOL stay as they are, and each settings.toml comment for the slot is reworded to say it also governs how returns are collected. No new slot has to be declared in three settings.toml files and pass the slot-declaration check. The waiting sentence fills the one host-varying paragraph that already says how returns are handled as they land. The Codex rule that closes an agent only after its pipeline has finished, then dispatches the next pending question, stays in the same paragraph as the batching it now depends on, so the two cannot drift apart. Each value now mixes two concerns, how many agents are in flight and when returns are collected, so the slot's name and comment no longer describe all of it. Every host's value changes even where only the waiting half differs, so giving Antigravity or Codex a different waiting form than Claude Code means rewriting the whole concurrency paragraph for that host. How much the Codex value grows depends on the axis the Codex wait form question owns.

A new slot of its own (for example ALTERNATIVES_WAIT) holds only the waiting sentence. Hosts with a blocking wait get the wait-once-then-batch form, and a host without one gets the batch-per-wake-up form. All three hosts declare it, and it is used once in core/skills/provide-alternatives-to-all-open-questions/SKILL.md as its own paragraph where the batch pipeline opens. ALTERNATIVES_CONCURRENCY is cut back to how many dispatches run at once (all together, or the Codex thread cap with close-and-refill) and drops its "as it lands" wording. The other three alternatives slots are unchanged. Each slot holds one concern, and the waiting sentence becomes exactly the one host slot the goal describes, with the per-wake-up form as one of its values. A host's waiting form can then change, for example Antigravity or Codex moving between the single-wait and per-wake-up forms, without touching its concurrency wording. A fourth alternatives slot has to be declared identically across three settings.toml files and used in core/, and the concurrency values still change because their "as it lands" wording must go. Codex's close-and-refill rule depends on when a question's batch has finished, so its two slot values have to be read together and can drift apart in a later edit, depending on the axis the Codex wait form question owns.

The waiting sentence is appended to the existing ALTERNATIVES_DISPATCH slot, which already names each host's agent tool (the Agent tool, spawn_agent). The wait sits beside the dispatch call as part of that host's tool-specific mechanics. ALTERNATIVES_CONCURRENCY keeps its count wording minus "as it lands". No new slot is declared. Each host's tool names sit in one value: the dispatch tool and the tool or loop it waits with. A reader of one host's settings.toml finds the whole dispatch-and-collect mechanism in one place, again without declaring a new slot. That slot ends where the dispatch prompt's fenced block opens, so the waiting sentence would come before the prompt whose returns it waits for, and its comment would have to be redefined. It mixes run control with the description of what the prompt carries, which the re-dispatch repair reuses as "the same prompt". The concurrency wording also still has to change, so the change touches two slots anyway.

No slot carries the waiting wording. Shared prose in core/ states it as a capability test that the runner applies at run time: where the host offers a blocking wait, wait once and batch; where it does not, batch at each wake-up. This mirrors the "where the host can run several agent dispatches at once" phrasing already inside the concurrency values. ALTERNATIVES_CONCURRENCY drops its "as it lands" wording and otherwise keeps its count wording. No slot is added or widened. No host has to be classified at build time. Antigravity, whose return delivery the repository does not record, and Codex, with no waiting tool named anywhere, each fall into the right branch by what the runner actually finds. The Claude Code and Antigravity trees stay byte-identical without assuming either host has a wait. It rejects the goal's own statement that the waiting sentence is the one host slot, so it needs a goal revision first. It also leaves to the runner's judgment during each run a choice that build-time slot values would otherwise settle for good. Whether it is still worth doing depends on the axes the Codex wait form and Antigravity wait form questions own.
